p.seg: One who is disliked yet cannot be faulted is
one who has attained righteousness (yì).
One who is faulted
yet cannot be disliked is
one who is sincere in benevolence (rén).
One whose actions do not go to excess is
one who knows the Way (dào).
One who, upon hearing the Way (dào), turns to those above, is
one who associates with superiors.
One who, upon hearing the Way (dào), turns to those below, is
one who associates with subordinates.
One who, upon hearing, turns inward to the self, is
one who cultivates the self.
Associating with superiors is close to serving a ruler;
associating with subordinates and winning over
the people is close to engaging in governance;
cultivating the self is close to attaining perfect benevolence (rén).
To associate with those who share the same principles is to do so
by means of the Way (dào).
To associate with those who do not share the same principles is to do so
by means of righteousness (yì).
To associate with those who take pleasure in the same things is to do so
by means of virtue (dé).
To associate with those who do not take pleasure in the same things is to do so
by means of calculation (móu).
In ordering what is within the gates,
one desires
ease.
In ordering what is outside the gates,
one desires regulation.
Seven.
In all cases of pleasing others, do not be grudging;
your actions must accord with this,
One
Although ordinary people possess an inborn nature (xìng),
their heart-mind (xīn) has no settled intent.
They await external things before they are roused,
they await pleasure before they act,
and they await habituation before they become
settled.
The dispositions of joy, anger, sorrow, and grief
are the inborn nature.
When they manifest externally,
it is because external things have drawn them out.
The inborn nature issues from the life-endowment (mìng),
and the life-endowment
descends from Heaven (tiān).
The Way (dào) begins with the feelings (qíng),
and the feelings arise from the inborn nature.
The starting point is close to the feelings.
the final stage is close to righteousness.
One who understands the emotions is able to
express them;
one who understands righteousness is able to internalize them.
Likes and dislikes
are part of human nature.
The objects of one's likes and dislikes
are external things.
The capacity for good
and not-good
is part of human nature,
but what is deemed good and what is deemed not-good
is a matter of circumstance.
In all cases, human nature is the host,
and external things are what it selects.
Metal and stone possess sound,
but if not struck, they do not
ring.
Although a person has an inborn nature,
if the mind does not engage it, it does not emerge.
The mind always has intent.
Without an object of engagement, it cannot act;
the mind cannot
operate on its own,
just as the mouth cannot speak on its own.
An ox is born and grows;
a wild goose is born and stretches.
Their nature makes it so.
That a person
learns, however,
is because something causes it to be so.
Of all things, there are none that are not different.
A pillar is something hard,
and one selects it for its hardness.
A binding cord is something
pliable,
and one selects it for its pliability.
Within the four seas, the inborn nature of people is the same.
Yet their use of the mind is different in each case;
teaching causes this to be so.
In all cases, the inborn nature may
be stimulated,
or obstructed,
or interacted with,
or honed,
or brought out,
or nourished,
or developed.
That which
stimulates the inborn nature
is external things.
That which obstructs the inborn nature
is pleasure.
That which interacts with the inborn nature
is custom.
That which hones the inborn nature...
is righteousness;
That which issues from one's nature,
is circumstance;
That which nurtures one's nature,
is habit;
That which develops one's nature,
is the Way.
All that is seen is called an 'object'.
That which is pleasing to oneself is called 'pleasure'.
That which
controls things is called 'circumstance'.
That which involves deliberate action is called 'cause'.
As for righteousness,
it is the summation of all that is good.
As for habit,
it is the means by which one habituates one's nature.
The Way is
the Way of the myriad things.
In all Ways,
the arts of the mind are primary.
The Way has four arts,
yet only
the Way of man can be followed as a Way.
As for the other three arts,
one can only speak of them, and that is all.
Two.
The *Shī* (Odes), the *Shū* (Documents), the *Lǐ* (Rites), and the *Yuè* (Music)—
their origins all arise
from man.
The *Shī*
are created for a purpose.
The *Shū*
are spoken for a purpose.
The *Lǐ* and the *Yuè*
are performed for a purpose.
The `shèngrén` (sage) groups them by
category and brings them together for discussion,
observes their sequence and provides instruction on them,
comprehends their meaning and arranges them in order,
and manages
their essential nature and determines their application,
and only then, in turn, uses them to teach.
Teaching
is that by which virtue is generated within.
Three.
The *Lǐ*
arise from the emotions,
or are otherwise stimulated into being;
they are formulated in response to specific affairs and in accordance with the circumstances.
The order of their sequence is the principle of appropriateness.
The ordering of these into
articulated rules is measure.
As for one's demeanor,
it is that by which one applies standards and regulations.
The noble person (jūnzǐ) esteems his inner feelings,
treasures righteousness,
perfects his regulations,
is fond of his demeanor,
delights in the Way,
and is pleased with its teachings;
for this reason, he is reverent.
Bowing
is the means by which one shows submission;
its form
is a matter of standard.
Gifts of silk (bìbó)
are the means by which one shows trustworthiness and gives a token;
their presentation
is a matter of the way of righteousness (yì dào).
Smiling
is the shallow lustre of ritual (lǐ).
Music (yuè)
is the deep lustre of ritual (lǐ).
In all sounds,
if their issuing from the inner feelings is authentic,
then their entering and stirring the hearts of others will be profound.
When one hears the sound of laughter,
one feels brightened and thereupon is joyful.
When one hears songs and ballads,
one feels uplifted and thus is stirred.
Listening to the sounds of the qín and sè zithers,
one's heart flutters and one thus feels apprehensive.
Watching the *Lài* and the *Wǔ* dances,
one feels solemn and thus is roused to action.
Watching the *Sháo* and the *Xià* dances,
one feels encouraged to strive
and thus becomes restrained.
Chanting with deep thought moves the heart,
and one sighs deeply.
Its adherence to rhythm is traditional;
its return to the good and reversion to the beginning is
cautious;
its entry [into the listener] is smooth.
It takes its virtue as its main principle.
As for the music of Zhèng and Wèi,
its sounds are improper and give free rein to the passions.
All ancient music harmonizes the heart;
beneficial music harmonizes the intent.
Both serve to instruct their people.
The *Lài* and the *Wǔ* are music of conquest;
the *Sháo* and the *Xià* are music of human sentiment.
When joy reaches its extreme, it must turn to sorrow;
crying is also sorrow.
In both, emotion has reached its extreme.
Sorrow and joy,
their natures are close to one another.
therefore the states of mind
they produce are not far apart.
When weeping moves the heart,
it is a gradual fading away.
Its pang is one of lingering attachment,
and it concludes in a state of mournfulness.
When music moves the heart,
it is profound, deep, swelling, and surging.
Its pang, in turn, is like a flowing current, resulting in sorrow,
and it leaves one in a state of far-reaching contemplation.
In all cases, sorrow follows from melancholic thought,
and joy follows from happy thought.
In any kind of contemplation, the exertion of the mind is the most intense part.
*Nǎn* (awe),
is the mode of this contemplation.
When the sound changes, the mind changes;
when the mind changes,
so too does the sound.
Moaning comes from sorrow,
clamor comes from joy,
chirping comes from the physical voice,
and heartfelt utterance comes from the mind.
Delight leads to exultation;
exultation leads to being stirred to action;
being stirred to action leads to physical movement;
physical movement leads to patterned action;
and patterned action leads to dance.
Dance...
is the culmination of joy.
When there is vexation, then there is worry.
When there is worry, then there is sorrow.
When there is sorrow, then there is distress.
When there is distress, then there is fear.
When there is fear, then one stamps the feet.
Stamping the feet,
is the culmination of vexation.
Five
For all who study, seeking to understand their heart-mind is difficult.
By following their actions,
one comes close to grasping it.
But this is not as quick as using music.
Even if one is capable in the action
but cannot master its inner intention,
it is not valued.
If in seeking its inner intention there is falsity,
one will not grasp it.
That a person cannot succeed with falsity
can be known.
If their faults appear ten times,
their true intention must lie therein.
By examining what is revealed,
how can the truth of the matter be missed?
Examination,
is the method of rightness.
Rightness,
is the way to reverence (jìng).
Reverence (jìng)
is the proper measure for things.
Genuineness
is the way to benevolence (rén).
Benevolence (rén)
is the way of nature (xìng).
Nature (xìng) sometimes gives rise to it.
Conscientiousness (zhōng) is the way to
trustworthiness (xìn)
Trustworthiness (xìn)
is the way to genuine feelings (qíng).
Genuine feelings (qíng) emerge from nature (xìng).
There are seven types of love;
only love rooted in one's nature is close to benevolence (rén).
There are five types of wisdom;
only [wisdom of]
the Way of righteousness (yì) is close to conscientiousness (zhōng).
There are three types of aversion;
hating what is not benevolent is close to righteousness (yì).
Of the four things that are taken as the Way (dào),
only the Way of humans is
a Way that can be truly followed.
For anyone who uses their mind with agitation,
overthinking is the worst of it.
For anyone who uses their intelligence rashly,
misfortune is the worst result.
For those whose use of the emotions is
extreme,
their sorrow and joy will be excessive.
For those whose use of the body is versatile,
their pleasures will be excessive.
For those who exhaust their strength,
their gains will be excessive.
The eye's love of
beautiful sights
and the ear's delight in sounds
are a dense and overflowing energy;
people will not hesitate to die for them.
When a person's conduct is meticulously principled,
if they do not have a discerning heart, it becomes mere superficial display.
When a person's conduct is discerning,
if they do not have a steadfast and foundational resolve, it becomes aimless.
For a person of clever
words and sharp phrases,
if they do not have a modest and self-restrained heart, their speech becomes dissolute.
For a person who is pleasant and with whom one can be harmonious and at peace,
if they do not have a disposition for striving
and accomplishment, they will be slighted.
When a person's character is straightforward and quick,
they must be guided.
When a person's character is profound,
they are insufficient without support.
In all people, rapacity is detestable.
To be rapacious is to be stingy,
miserliness leads to anxious calculation,
and anxious calculation leads to no one forming a bond
with them.
Prudence
is the way of benevolence.
However, its faults are not detested.
Quickness
is the way of strategy;
if it results in a fault, there is blame.
That a person who is not prudent will have faults
is indeed true.
The genuine feelings of any person are pleasing.
If one acts with sincerity,
even if a fault is made, it is not detested;
if one does not act with sincerity,
even if a difficult task is accomplished, it is not valued.
If one has sincerity,
even before they have acted,
they will be trusted.
To be trusted without having spoken
is the mark of one who has excellent sincerity.
For the people to be constant without instruction
is the mark of those whose nature is good.
For the people to be encouraged without rewards
is the mark of a ruler who contains blessings.
When the people are in awe without punishments being applied,
this is one who possesses
an awe-inspiring heart.
Though he is of low status, the people esteem him;
this is one who possesses virtue.
Though he is poor, the people gather to him;
this is one who possesses the Way.
To be joyful when dwelling alone;
this is characteristic of one who has internalized ritual propriety.
When you speak of it, then be
clear.
When you recommend them, do so without reservation.
In all associations, do not be without end;
you must ensure they have a proper conclusion.
In all cases of being summoned, do not be fearful;
do not speak alone.
When you are
alone, practice what your father and elder brothers enjoy.
If there is no great harm,
it is acceptable to bend a little to participate.
Once it is done, do not speak of it again.
In all matters of trouble and adversity, one should want to take responsibility.
樂事欲後。 In all matters of sorrow and trouble, one should seek to take them on; in joyful matters, one should place oneself last.
身欲靜而毋憾， Your self should be tranquil and without regret.
慮欲淵而毋𢠿， Your thoughts should be profound and not shallow.
行欲勇而必至， Your actions should be brave and must reach their goal.
貌欲壯而毋拔， Your demeanor should be dignified and not flighty.
心欲柔齊而泊， Your mind should be gentle, even-tempered, and tranquil.
喜欲智而亡末， Your joy should be wise and not lead to excess.
樂欲懌而又有志， Your pleasure should be gladdening and yet have purpose.
憂欲斂而毋昏， Your sorrow should be restrained and not muddled.
怒欲浧而毋希， Your anger should be settled and not diffuse.
進欲遜而毋巧， When advancing, one should be modest and not artful.
退欲尋而毋輕， When retreating, one should be deliberate and not rash.
欲皆度而毋𢠿。 Your desires should all be measured and not shallow.
八
君子執志必有夫廣廣之心， Eight. The gentleman, in holding to his aspirations, must have a broad and expansive heart.
出言必有
夫柬柬之信， When speaking, he must have a trustworthiness that is discerning and sincere.
賓客之禮必有夫齊齊之容， In the rites for receiving guests, he must have a solemn and composed demeanor.
祭祀之禮必有夫齊齊之敬， In the rites of sacrifice, he must have a solemn and reverent respect.
居喪必有夫戀戀之哀。 When in mourning, he must have a lingering and reluctant sorrow.
君子身以為主心。 For the gentleman, the self takes the mind as its master.
